# Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square in Q2 2026: 14 stocks, three new payment and data names, and Alphabet sold

By Gabriel Zacarkim · Published Oct 11, 2026 · Data as of Oct 9, 2026 close (positions as of June 30, 2026)

Pershing Square Capital Management, the firm Bill Ackman founded and runs, filed its 13F for the second quarter of 2026 on August 14. It lists 14 U.S.-listed stocks worth $19.47 billion on June 30, 2026, up from 11 positions and $14.28 billion three months earlier. It is one of the most concentrated portfolios among the 38 managers this site tracks: the seven largest positions are 76.8% of the total. The full list is on Bill Ackman’s page.

Each block is a position, sized by its value on June 30, 2026. Green: new or added; red: reduced; grey: unchanged. Hover or tap a block for the numbers.

## What changed

Four companies entered the portfolio: Visa, Mastercard and S&P Global — around 5.5% each — and Netflix at 4.8%. None of Pershing Square’s 13F filings since 2016 had held Visa, Mastercard or S&P Global; Netflix is a return, since the firm held it in the first quarter of 2022. Ackman added to Meta (+20.1% in shares), Uber (+14.6%), Restaurant Brands (+14.0%) and Microsoft (+9.8%), and cut Amazon by a quarter. Alphabet, a small position of $98.7 million (0.7%) in March across its two share classes, was sold entirely.

A 13F shows holdings at the end of the quarter. It does not say on which day a position was opened, and a “new” line means the shares were held on June 30 — not necessarily that they were bought on the market.

## A position in its own fund

One of the new lines is Pershing Square USA, Ltd. (PSUS), a closed-end fund managed by Pershing Square Capital Management that listed on the New York Stock Exchange in April 2026 at $50.00 a share. The 4,000,000 shares in the 13F are the manager’s own investment in the fund: according to the prospectus, an affiliate committed to an aggregate investment of $200 million at $50.00 a share in the private placement that accompanied the offering, and agreed not to sell $100 million of it for 25 years. At the June 30 price of $37.38 the stake was worth $149.5 million. It is not a purchase on the open market.

## Companies with ties to the manager

Howard Hughes Holdings is more than a holding: the PSUS prospectus says Ackman has been executive chairman of its board since May 2025 and describes Howard Hughes as one of the manager’s permanent capital vehicles. Seaport Entertainment Group, the much smaller position, has a member of Pershing Square’s investment team, Anthony Massaro, on its board.

## The S&P Global spin-off after quarter-end

One day after the 13F date, on July 1, 2026, S&P Global completed the spin-off of Mobility Global (ticker MBGL), distributing one MBGL share for every S&P Global share held on the June 15 record date. Two practical consequences follow. First, price histories adjusted for the spin-off show S&P Global’s June 30 close at $385.30, while the actual price — the one that matches the 13F value — was $407.26. Second, anyone valuing the position today has to add the Mobility Global shares that came with it.

## The same shares at today’s prices

Repriced at the October 9, 2026 close — and assuming nothing changed since June 30, which the 13F cannot tell us — the 14 positions would be worth about $21.17 billion. The biggest moves since June 30 were in Microsoft (+43.4%) and Meta (+27.6%), while Brookfield (−12.9%), Seaport (−16.4%) and Hertz (−15.2%) fell. The next 13F, for the third quarter, is due by mid-November.

A 13F covers only U.S.-listed long positions: it does not show short positions, shares listed outside the United States, cash or other assets, so it is Pershing Square’s U.S. stock portfolio rather than everything the firm owns. None of this is investment advice.

Ackman's Q2 2026 Overhaul: Six New Positions and Two Big Exits at Pershing Square — InvestorLens — InvestorLens

October 21, 2026

# Ackman's Q2 2026 Overhaul: Six New Positions and Two Big Exits at Pershing Square

Pershing Square's Q2 2026 13F shows Bill Ackman adding Visa, Mastercard and Netflix while exiting Alphabet and Universal Music.

Few concentrated portfolios change shape as dramatically as Bill Ackman's. Pershing Square's Q2 2026 13F, covering the quarter ended June 30, showed one of its biggest reshuffles in a while: six new positions, two full exits, and meaningful moves in the largest holdings. Here is what the filing shows and how to read it.

## The new positions

According to press coverage of the filing, Pershing Square opened six new positions: Visa (V), Mastercard (MA), Netflix (NFLX), S&P Global (SPGI), Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), and Alcon.

Visa and Mastercard each came in at roughly $1.1 billion, and Netflix at about $934 million. Sizes for the other three were not widely reported. Even so, the theme is clear: payment networks, financial data and exchange infrastructure, plus one consumer-media franchise. These are businesses with recurring, toll-road style revenue, which is a hallmark of Ackman's long-standing preference for simple, predictable, dominant companies.

The Netflix entry is worth a closer look. Reports noted the stock traded around 26 times earnings, below its five-year average closer to 36x, after a roughly 32% decline over the prior year. That is a classic pattern for a concentrated value-oriented buyer: a high-quality business at a de-rated multiple. If you want to see which other large managers hold or have exited Netflix, our overlap tool shows it side by side.

## The exits

Two positions disappeared entirely. Alphabet (GOOGL) was sold in full, and so was Universal Music Group, a stake worth about $1.5 billion. Fully exiting a position that size is a strong signal, because a manager running a roughly 12 to 15 name book cannot afford idle capital. Every dollar in one name is a dollar not in another.

## Trims and adds in the core

Amazon was cut by more than 25% but not eliminated. It remains a top-four holding at around $2.0 billion, or about 10% of the disclosed portfolio. Microsoft went the other way: Pershing added roughly 10% to bring it to about $2.3 billion, around 12% of the portfolio, making it slightly larger than Amazon.

This is a good reminder that a 13F is a snapshot of changes, not a verdict. Trimming a winner can be about position sizing and risk, not a loss of conviction. Adding to Microsoft while trimming Amazon looks more like rebalancing within the mega-cap bucket than an exit from it.

## How to use this signal

A few cautions apply before copying any 13F move:

- The data is lagged. The filing reflects June 30 holdings and was published in mid-August. Prices and the manager's own views may have moved since. See our guide on using the 13F lag.
- A 13F shows only long US equity positions. It omits shorts, most derivatives and non-US holdings, so it is never the whole portfolio.
- Concentration cuts both ways. Ackman's high-conviction sizing means each change is meaningful, but it also means results are lumpy.

A useful way to apply this is to check whether the new Pershing names appear elsewhere. If payment networks or exchange operators are also being added by other top managers, that is a sector-level signal rather than a single-manager idea. Our investors page lets you browse each manager's holdings, the flow page shows where capital is moving quarter to quarter, and the macro consensus view rolls up positioning across the whole group.

## The takeaway

Pershing Square's Q2 move rotated away from Alphabet and Universal Music, trimmed Amazon, added to Microsoft, and rebuilt around payments, financial infrastructure and a de-rated streaming leader. Whether or not you agree with the bets, the pattern is consistent with how Ackman has always invested: own a handful of dominant businesses, and act decisively when price and quality diverge. The next filing, covering Q3, is due in mid-November, and it will show whether these positions were built up further or left alone.

Bill Ackman Is Directing Up to $3 Billion Into Howard Hughes' Insurance Arm, Vantage, as Part of His Plan to Build a Modern Berkshire Hathaway. Is HHH Stock the Way to Play His Buffett Ambitions? | The Motley Fool

Ever since Warren Buffett built Berkshire Hathaway around ownership of insurance companies, many have attempted to copy his approach. Unlike traditional insurance stocks, which seek to profit by investing insurance premiums in fixed-income instruments such as bonds, Buffett's approach entails investing float in stocks to generate superior long-term returns.

Investor Bill Ackman, through Howard Hughes Holdings (HHH +1.01%), or HHH for short, is the latest Wall Street titan to try to emulate this strategy. Not only that, but Ackman appears to be aiming to mimic the approach of another famed investment holding company.

Pershing Square Capital Management CEO Bill Ackman. Image source: Getty Images.

## Ackman, Howard Hughes, and the Vantage Deal

Howard Hughes Holdings was formed in 2010, when then-bankrupt General Growth Properties spun off its real estate development business. Known for master-planned community developments like Summerlin, located outside Las Vegas, the company has slowly shifted its focus since Bill Ackman's involvement began in the late 2010s. First, by spinning off non-core real estate and other assets as Seaport Entertainment in 2024.

Then, in 2025, Pershing Square invested another $900 million in HHH, raising the fund's stake to 47%. Still working slowly, Ackman has only recently revealed his "master plan" for the master-planned communities company. In a recent interview with Bloomberg, Ackman discussed plans to transform HHH into both a Berkshire-style insurance holding company and an asset manager akin to Brookfield and Blackstone.

First, in a Berkshire-esque move, HHH acquired Vantage for $2.1 billion. Vantage's book value of around $1.8 billion represents much of this valuation. Alongside the purchase price of Vantage, Howard Hughes Holdings plans to invest between $2.5 billion and $3 billion of its excess free cash flow into the insurance unit over the next five years. HHH's goal is to have most of Vantage's excess capital invested in stocks. Ackman's Pershing Square will also manage Vantage's portfolio for free.

Second, alongside the Buffett insurance gambit, Ackman also seeks to juice up Howard Hughes' returns from real estate investments by taking on third-party investors and charging them management fees similar to those that Brookfield and Blackstone charge for their respective real estate investment management subsidiaries.

## Is Howard Hughes Holdings a buy?

Howard Hughes Holdings shares surged around the time of Ackman's "Berkshire and Brookfield" remarks, but have since pulled back into the high-$60s per share, around the stock's book value of $66.95 per share. Yet while the stock may appear to have minimal downside at this price level, keep in mind that only time will tell whether Ackman's big plans pan out.

For one, it takes years, if not decades, to determine success in this area. Some insurers taking a Berkshire-style approach, like Markel Group, have beaten the market over a multidecade time frame; others, like Greenlight Capital, have lost money for investors.

In fact, Greenlight Capital, with excess funds managed by hedge fund billionaire David Einhorn, sounds very similar to what Ackman has in store for Howard Hughes Holdings. That's not to say a similar outcome is bound to happen, but consider this food for thought before investing just on the headlines alone.

Instead, consider waiting until some of the excitement surrounding Ackman's plans has simmered down. In the past, Howard Hughes Holdings has traded well below book value, and a similar situation could emerge again in the near term.

Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square Capital Management Sold Alphabet and Bought These 2 Beaten-Down Stocks | The Motley Fool

In investing, as in other aspects of life, it makes sense to take lessons from those who have been successful. One such person is Bill Ackman, the founder and CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management, a hedge fund that has produced excellent returns over the past couple of decades. During the second quarter, Ackman and his investing team made a move that probably took some investors by surprise: They closed their position in Alphabet (GOOG -1.08%) (GOOGL -1.24%), a tech leader that seems to be firing on all cylinders. 

What's more, Ackman bought more shares of Meta Platforms (META -0.96%), while initiating a position in Netflix (NFLX -1.79%), both of which have significantly lagged broader equities over the trailing-12-month period. The Alphabet move aside, Ackman's decision to go against the grain by investing in Meta and Netflix during the second quarter may have been a great move. Here is why.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

## 1. Meta Platforms

In the second quarter, Meta Platforms' revenue grew by a healthy 28% year over year to $60.8 billion. However, the company's earnings per share (EPS) dropped 13% year over year to $6.18, and its free cash flow came in at $784 million, significantly down from the $8.5 billion reported in the year-ago period. Meta's hefty artificial intelligence (AI)-related investments are helping improve its ad business, but they are weighing on margins and profits, at least for now, and that's spooking some investors. Further, Meta is facing lawsuits over social media harm.

Meta has other potential growth avenues, including selling excess AI computing capacity, a business with strong current demand. On the legal front, Meta recently reached an agreement to settle many of its social media harm lawsuits for a rather modest amount, considering how much money it makes. So, despite recent struggles, the stock remains a great long-term pick. 

## 2. Netflix

Netflix's business has matured, and the company now faces more competition than it once did. As a result, engagement on its platform is no longer as strong, while its financial results have been unimpressive. Can Netflix bounce back? One thing to note is that there is still a massive addressable market across streaming and advertising. Cable isn't dead, far from it, but the cord-cutting trend should continue over the long run.

As more people switch to streaming, Netflix remains well-positioned to benefit. Also, Netflix has encountered somewhat similar problems before. Growing competition and lower-than-expected engagement are nothing new. In the past, it has found ways to get things back on track. Could Netflix do so again? According to reports, the company is considering granting its users access to other streaming platforms through its app.

# Bill Ackman Takes Another Swing At NFLX After Colossal 2022 Loss: 'Netflix Has Effectively Won The Streaming Wars'

The founder and CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management has said that the hedge fund has picked up a new stake in Netflix in the latest quarter.

Bill Ackman attends Legion of Honour Award Ceremony and Dinner for Olivia Tournay Flatto at the Park Avenue Armory on October 19, 2022 in New York City. (Photo by Sylvain Gaboury/Patrick McMullan via Getty Images)

Aashika Suresh· Stocktwits

 Updated Aug 13, 2026 | 4:20 AM EDT

- In 2022, the investor sold NFLX shares after holding it for just three months, clocking a loss of more than $400 million after the stock plunged due to losing subscribers for the first time in a decade.
- The hedge fund now believes that Netflix has since effectively won the streaming wars.
- Pershing Square noted that Netflix is now the dominant global streaming platform, lauded its content discipline and cash position, and also highlighted the buying opportunity after shares fell about 50% from their June 2025 highs. 

Billionaire investor William Ackman is taking a chance once again on Netflix Inc. (NFLX) by acquiring a fresh stake in the streaming giant through Pershing Square Holdings Ltd. (PS), the publicly traded investment vehicle managed by the Pershing Square investment firm.

This is Ackman’s second time investing in the company. In 2022, the investor sold NFLX shares after holding it for just three months, clocking a loss of more than $400 million. However, the stock managed to rebound spectacularly, having risen nearly 650% since then, driven by a password-sharing crackdown, the introduction of a cheaper ad-supported subscription tier, and a move into live content and sports. 

Anushka Basu

“When we first invested in early 2022, investors feared an escalating content arms race among a crowded field of streaming entrants. At the same time, cash content spend substantially exceeded content amortization, weighing on free cash flow. The launch of a previously disavowed advertising tier added further uncertainty,” Pershing Square said in its latest Investment Manager’s Report. 

“Netflix has since effectively won the streaming wars,” it added. 

## Why Ackman Sold Netflix In 2022

In April 2022, Netflix reported its first subscriber loss in a decade, losing about 200,000 subscribers in the first quarter. The suspension of service in Russia amid the onset of the Ukraine war hit the company hard, costing it about 700,000 members. 

The stock plunged 35%, prompting Ackman’s Pershing Square to sell its 3.1 million shares for a loss of more than $400 million. Ackman acknowledged that Netflix’s planned moves to introduce advertising and crack down on password sharing made strategic sense but would make the business harder to predict in the near term. 

Since Pershing Square concentrates its portfolio in roughly a dozen companies and requires a high degree of predictability, Ackman said at the time that he had “lost confidence” in the ability “to predict the company's future prospects with a sufficient degree of certainty." 

## What Makes Netflix Attractive Now?

Pershing Square noted that Netflix is now the dominant global streaming platform, boasting over 325 million subscribers, nearly double the combined base of its two closest competitors, Walt Disney’s (DIS) Disney+ and Warner Bros Discovery’s (WBD) HBO Max.

The firm also lauded Netflix’s content discipline, noting that cash content spend has grown at just a 2% annual rate since 2021, further noting that the streaming giant now converts approximately 90% of earnings into free cash flow, primarily redeployed into share buybacks. 

In its release, Pershing Square highlighted that Netflix’s advertising has scaled rapidly toward $3 billion, while its lower-priced ad-supported tier broadens the addressable market among price-conscious consumers, particularly in international markets. 

“Our opportunity arose after Netflix’s share price fell ~50% from its June 2025 high of $134, de-rating from over 40 times forward earnings per share to 21 times. The decline began with prolonged uncertainty around the company’s bid for Warner Bros. Discovery, which it ultimately lost in February 2026, enabling it to collect a $2.8 billion termination fee. Investor focus has since shifted to plateauing engagement trends and the longer-term risk AI-generated video poses to content creation,” the firm said. 

The firm also argued that short-form video is taking share mainly from linear TV and weaker streaming services, not Netflix. Pershing believes AI risks are overstated, as producing high-quality long-form content remains costly, while Netflix’s scale and AI-powered recommendations, as well as ad targeting, could strengthen its competitive edge.

# Pershing Square holds $934 million Netflix stake after re-entry

Key Highlights

- Pershing Square holds 13,081,465 Netflix shares valued at $934 million
- The stake represents approximately 4.8% of Pershing Square's total assets
- Bill Ackman cited improved cash flow generation and dominant market position as key reasons for re-entry
- The fund previously exited Netflix in 2022 due to concerns over its unproven advertising business

Pershing Square Capital Management holds a $934 million stake in Netflix Inc (NASDAQ: NFLX) as of the end of the second quarter, marking a significant re-entry into the streaming giant. The position comprises 13,081,465 shares, representing approximately 4.8% of the hedge fund's total assets.

## Strategic rationale for re-entry

Bill Ackman, founder of Pershing Square, cited Netflix's "dominant position" and enhanced cash flow generation as primary drivers for the investment. The firm had previously exited its Netflix position in 2022 due to concerns over the company's expansion into the unproven advertising business.

Since that exit, Ackman noted that Netflix has successfully built a robust advertising segment and won the "streaming wars." He emphasized that the company is now significantly more cash flow generative than it was during the initial holding period.

"At a price that made sense, we bought it back," Ackman stated on The Knowledge Podcast. He added that Netflix remains incredibly well positioned to innovate and serves as the standard for the streaming industry.

## Market timing and valuation context

The re-entry follows a period of volatility for Netflix shares. After soaring from 2022 to 2025, the stock began declining in late 2025 and continued to fall into early 2026. Ackman indicated that this downward trend provided an attractive entry point for Pershing Square.

Bill Ackman Sold His Remaining Alphabet Shares and Bought This Streaming Stock

# Bill Ackman Sold His Remaining Alphabet Shares and Bought This Streaming Stock

 Habib Ur Rehman September 8, 2026 3 min read

Bill Ackman's Q2 portfolio changes are drawing fresh attention on September 7: Pershing Square exited its remaining Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ: GOOGL) shares and established a position in Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ: NFLX). The pair offers two different ways to monetize AI, with very different demands on cash. 

## What the filings actually show 

At Q1's end, Pershing reported 32,376 Alphabet Class A shares and 311,726 Class C shares. Its Q2 parent-company filing contained neither class, alongside 13,081,465 Netflix shares valued at $934 million. The manager explicitly moved its reporting into the parent's filing. These are quarter-end disclosures, not September trades, and they do not identify which sale funded which purchase. 

Bill Ackman Sold His Remaining Alphabet Shares and Bought This Streaming Stock 

Netflix, Inc. (NASDAQ:NFLX) is using AI to improve discovery, advertising and production. Its July 16 shareholder letter described those applications and maintained an approximately $3 billion full-year advertising revenue forecast. Better targeting and more accessible ad buying can increase the value of viewing hours without requiring a matching increase in content spending. 

Pershing's investment letter argues that Netflix's scale and slower content-cost growth support expanding margins. The challenge is sustaining engagement and pricing: Netflix's Q3 revenue forecast implies 11.7% growth, below Q2's 13.4%. Its second-quarter free cash flow also fell to $1.5 billion, partly reflecting higher tax payments associated with the Warner termination fee. 

Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) has more direct infrastructure exposure. Google Cloud revenue grew 82% in Q2, and Alphabet's operating income increased 30%. That demand supports continued investment, but $44.9 billion of quarterly capital expenditures exceeded operating cash flow, producing negative $5.9 billion of free cash flow. Returns on the new capacity must justify the cash consumed today. 

## Ackman's view is one among many 

Insider Monkey's database showed 275 Alphabet Class A holders in Q2 2026 versus 265 in Q1, up ten. Berkshire increased its Class A shares approximately 45%, even as Pershing eliminated its residual position. Netflix's count fell 23 to 121 from 144; Pershing's position was newly established, so a percentage increase from zero is undefined. 

Netflix had 90,512,500 shares sold short at August 14, or 2.20% of float and three days to cover. That snapshot describes outstanding positions, not their motives. 

Netflix offers a more direct route from AI improvements to advertising returns, though slowing growth tests execution. Alphabet's faster cloud expansion brings greater funding demands and more dependence on sustained utilization of expensive capacity. Ackman's trade sharpens that comparison; subsequent margins and cash conversion will determine how well either opportunity rewards shareholders. 

While we acknowledge the potential of GOOGL and NFLX as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. Bill Ackman Has 45% of His New Hedge Fund's Portfolio Invested in Just 3 Incredible Growth Stocks | The Motley Fool

Bill Ackman is known for managing a highly concentrated portfolio with just a handful of high-conviction stock picks. So, when he launched a new closed-end fund earlier this year, it was a safe bet to think he would buy stocks that mostly match the portfolio held by Pershing Square's (PS -2.20%) other fund, Pershing Square Holdings.

Investors got their first glimpse at Ackman's purchases for Pershing Square USA (PSUS -0.19%) last month in his first letter to shareholders since launching the fund. Ackman says the timing of the launch worked out well, as the market provided an opportunity to buy into some of the most promising businesses right now. He quickly deployed nearly all of the capital raised in the fund's IPO, and three of the purchases now account for roughly 45% of the portfolio based on last month's update.

Image source: Getty Images.

## Microsoft (17.9% of assets)

Microsoft (MSFT +0.66%) is both a leading enterprise software company and a cloud platform-as-a-service provider. Both businesses have benefited from the increased capabilities of artificial intelligence over the last few years.

Ackman argues that Microsoft's core Microsoft 365 software suite is far more resilient to potential AI disruption than other software. In fact, Microsoft's Copilot AI is seeing excellent traction, garnering more than 30 million paid subscribers, with subscriber additions more than doubling sequentially last quarter. That's enabled it to produce strong revenue growth for the segment, up 14% year over year last quarter.

Microsoft's Azure cloud computing segment gets all the attention these days, though. The company is spending heavily to expand capacity for AI training and inference. Management expects to spend $175 billion during calendar 2026, plus additional expenses for operating leases. With remaining performance obligations totaling $678 billion (and growing) across its software suite and its cloud computing business, it can easily support that level of spending.

Microsoft stock has pushed higher in recent months, but the shares remain attractive at 25 times forward earnings. Ackman expects the company to grow earnings per share at a compound rate of about 19% over the next three to five years, which should allow for significantly more price appreciation.

## Meta Platforms (14.7%)

Meta Platforms (META -0.96%) is "one of the clearest beneficiaries of AI," Ackman wrote in his most recent letter to shareholders. That's most evident in the revenue acceleration exhibited in Meta's core advertising business. Ad sales climbed 30% in the first half of 2026, up from 22% in 2025.

Meta's advancements in AI help improve its recommendation algorithms, which drive both engagement and ad efficacy. That shows up as an increase in both ad impressions and average price per ad, leading to very strong results.

Meta's at a distinct advantage in terms of distribution of its AI features. Its Meta AI chatbot quickly gained 1 billion users thanks to integration with its messaging apps and Instagram. It could see similar adoption for Muse with WhatsApp integration. Other potential AI-related revenues include business chatbots, which could enable more consumer-business interaction on its messaging apps.
